ops.label: DBMS — a database is a collection of tables
ops.detail: Database Management System. The interesting word is management: storing the values is the easy half. An HR database would hold an employees table, a salary table and a job history table — one subject area, several tables, one database.

ops.detail: Which table connects to which, and through what.

ops.label: All three together = the schema
ops.detail: A properly defined outline of what the data looks like. A file has no notion of any of it. The DBMS is not storage — it is the layer that knows the shape of what is stored.

ops.label: Access is a permissions boundary, not a technical one
ops.detail: Organisations run many databases and the sensitive ones are walled off — you would not be given the HR database, because salary sits there. The instructor's own example: LinkedIn stores user chats and he has no access to them. You are handed a subset someone else chose.

ops.label: RDBMS — tables connected by common fields
ops.detail: The relationship is the common field. Worked example: an employee table holding location type (remote/office) and a salary table holding amounts. Average salary by location type cannot be answered from either alone — the two must be combined, and that is only possible because the employee number appears in both. Remove the common field and the question is not hard, it is unanswerable. Almost every database met in practice is relational.

ops.markdown:
**Vendors:** Oracle, MySQL, SQLite, PostgreSQL.

**90% of the syntax stays the same across vendors.** The 10% that differs is **date syntax** — date functions are not standardised. Everything else is effectively the same.

Why that is the 10%: dates are the piece every vendor implemented its own way before anyone standardised them. So date handling is where muscle memory breaks on a switch — everything else transfers.

Analogies from class: knowing Chrome means you can use Edge or Firefox; knowing Excel means you can use Google Sheets. You are learning a language, not a product.

The instructor uses **Presto** at work — a name absent from the vendor list above, which makes the point.

ops.title: Why a database and not Excel

cells.c-arg: Anything Excel does, SQL does — but not on billions of rows. Scale is the whole distinction. VLOOKUP also cannot return multiple matches: three occurrences give you the first and silently drop the rest. A correctness problem, not a size one — it becomes a wrong answer, not an error message.

Demonstrated live, not asserted: a shared sheet, everyone told to enter name and email, a chocolate for whoever ended in the top row. People deleted each other's entries and someone inserted a row to jump the queue. With concurrent writers and no ownership, the file's contents become a function of who edited last, not of what is true.
Excel has essentially no built-in security. The test question: would you trust a company that stored your Instagram or LinkedIn password in a spreadsheet?

If everyone has edit access, the table is not a source of truth — a salesperson short of target could insert a sales entry and claim the commission, and nothing in the file would object. Databases distinguish reading from writing at all, which a shared sheet does not.
Databases are fast. Excel is not.
Only 1 and 5 are about the tool's capability. Reasons 2, 3 and 4 are all about many people touching the same data — that is the real argument.

ops.label: Read broadly, write nowhere
ops.detail: Asked in class: if you cannot edit, what can you do? You can view and extract the data and pull it to your own machine. You cannot change values in place. Edit access belongs to SQL developers — which is the shape of the analyst's job.

ops.detail: customer_zip is CHAR(6) "ideally" — the instructor's hedge. The reasoning is that a postal code cannot be aggregated, so it is text rather than a number.

No primary key of its own — a join table carrying other tables' ids. quantity is DECIMAL(16,2) because a farmer's market sells 2.5 kg; read that as 16 digits total with 2 decimals, not 16 before the point. Columns the lecture never typed are left untyped.

ops.markdown:
There is no inherent advantage either way. It depends on how you want the data constrained.

| Column | Type | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Customer name | `VARCHAR` | You cannot know how long a name will be |
| Country code `IND`, `AUS`, `PAK` | `CHAR(3)` | You want exactly three |
| Phone number | `CHAR(10)` | Text, not a number — and it must be exactly ten. A nine-digit phone number is unusable |
| Zip / postal code | `CHAR(6)` | Text, not a number, because you cannot aggregate a postal code |

**The deciding test.** Can you meaningfully add or average this? Averaging zip codes produces a
number that means nothing, so a zip is text. That test is what tells a digit string apart from a
number — not whether it is made of digits.

The lecture reads `DECIMAL(4,3)` as **4 digits before the point and 3 after** — `9999.999`.

**Standard SQL does not work that way.** `DECIMAL(p, s)` is *p total digits, of which s sit after
the point*. `DECIMAL(4,3)` permits `9.999` — one digit before the point, not four.

The class notes reproduce the instructor's version and then break off without resolving it, so there
is no second authority in the course material. Treat the lecture's reading as wrong.

**The consequence, on the schema beside this note.** `quantity DECIMAL(16,2)` is **16 digits in
total with 2 after the point**, not 16 before and 2 after. Read it the lecture's way and you would
believe that column holds eighteen digits.

Not from the lecture — the instructor treats "Float / Decimal" as one row meaning
"numbers with a decimal point" and never separates them. Recorded here because the distinction
decides which one you reach for.

They differ in one thing: **exact versus approximate.**

- **`DECIMAL(p, s)` is exact.** Stored in base 10, as the digits you wrote. `0.1 + 0.2` is exactly
  `0.3`. What goes in comes back out, to the last digit, within the declared precision.
- **`FLOAT` / `DOUBLE` is approximate.** Stored as binary floating point — a fixed number of
  significant bits plus an exponent. Most decimal fractions have no exact binary form, the way a
  third has no exact decimal form. `0.1 + 0.2` returns `0.30000000000000004`, and
  `WHERE price = 0.3` silently matches nothing.

The error is tiny per value and **accumulates across rows**.

**Which to use**

- **`DECIMAL` when a human will audit the number.** Money, prices, billed quantity, tax — anything
  summed and then reconciled against another system. The failure it prevents is a ledger off by a
  few paise across a million rows, with no way to find where.
- **`FLOAT` when the number was measured.** Temperatures, sensor readings, coordinates, ratios,
  model output — where magnitude matters and the fourth decimal is noise.

**The one-line test: counted or paid takes `DECIMAL`; measured takes `FLOAT`.**

This is also why `DECIMAL` takes a precision argument at all — being exact, it has to be told how
many digits to keep. `FLOAT` takes none, because it promises no specific digit.

**In BigQuery**, the exact types are `NUMERIC` / `BIGNUMERIC` and the approximate one is `FLOAT64`.
`FLOAT64` is what an upload will tend to land on, so a price column is worth checking after import.

Every column marked fk is a primary key in another table, which is the only condition; duplicates and nulls in them change nothing. quantity is DECIMAL(16,2) because a farmer's market sells 2.5 kg — 16 digits in total with 2 decimals, not 16 before the point. ops.markdown:
**The lecture's definition.** A combination of more than one column acting as a primary key —
unique plus not null — is a candidate key.

**The standard definition.** A candidate key is any *minimal* set of columns that could serve as the
primary key, **including a single column**. A key made of more than one column is specifically a
**composite key**.

So the lecture defines candidate key = composite key. The class notes and the recording agree with
each other, which means this is what was taught rather than a mishearing.

**Which to give.** The assessment wants the lecture's version. An interview wants the standard one.
Those are different audiences and the same answer will not serve both.

**His own caveat, worth keeping either way.** A multi-column key is not a good way to store data.
Every table you want to join to must then carry *both* columns, which grows the dataset and its
complexity. Ideally a table has one primary key column.

That caveat lands directly on the schema beside this note: `customer_purchases`, `vendor_inventory`
and `vendor_booth_assignments` each have no single-column primary key, so their identity is exactly
the multi-column arrangement he advises against.

**One thing not carried.** He says in passing that "nulls are not unique" and leaves it undeveloped.
Real engines differ on whether a unique constraint permits more than one null, and the lecture does
not establish it, so it is not recorded here as a rule.

Both quiz items tested the four keys, and both were widely missed — the same mistake in
mirror image.

**Q1 — Can an Aadhaar card be used as a primary key in an organization?**
**No. It is a unique key.** 61% of the batch answered yes. Not everyone holds an Aadhaar card, so
the column admits missing values, and missing values fail the not-null condition. Aadhaar numbers
are unique; that is only half of what a primary key requires.

**Q2 — Can a foreign key have nulls?**
**Yes, absolutely.** The only precondition for a foreign key is that the column is a primary key in
some *other* table. Given that, it may hold nulls, duplicates, anything. The instructor noted he has
never seen a fully correct answer on this one.

**The diagnosis, which is the part worth keeping.** The first miss drops a clause — "unique" fires
and the answer arrives before not-null is ever checked. The second adds a clause that was never
there — "keys must be unique and not null" gets imported from the primary key and attached to a
foreign key, which makes no claim about its own contents at all.

Both come from treating *key* as one concept with shared properties. It is not. A primary key makes
two claims, a unique key makes one, and a foreign key makes none about itself — its status belongs
entirely to another table.

ops.value: Unique + NOT NULL — the second half is the one that gets forgotten
A primary key in another table — and nothing else counts. Duplicates and nulls are fine

ops.title: What a primary key is actually for

ops.markdown:
**The main function of a primary key is not to relate to other tables.** It is to be the primary
identifier of records in its own table. Relating to another table is the foreign key's role.

§9 opens by defining a key as the common field that connects tables, and that framing invites reading
every key as relational. A primary key is not. It answers "which row is this one" inside a single
table, and it would still be needed if the database held exactly one table and no joins existed at
all.

The foreign key is the relational one, and it is defined entirely by pointing outward — its status is
a fact about another table, not about itself. The primary key points inward.
